extracted.intended_audience: policy makers, IP lawyers, IP offices and stakeholders working on geographical indications and IP enforcement in GCC countries and the EU
extracted.subtask_short: GIs protection and enforcement in GCC
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts legal standards, registration conditions, exclusions, enforcement measures and policy recommendations relating to geographical indications (GIs) and IP enforcement across GCC countries, with emphasis on compatibility with TRIPS, national laws, and possible EU cooperation. Useful for drafting, advising, or evaluating GI systems and enforcement in the GCC region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistrable signs that mislead as to origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks that create confusion with regard to the origin or source of goods or services (including geographical names and data) are unregistrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: "geographical names and data if their use would create confusion with regard to the origin or source of goods or services." (cites GCC Unified Trademark Law). Also: trademarks that are likely to mislead the public or trade circles as regards the geographical origin or that contain false information are not eligible for protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: GIs may be registered as collective or certification marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that can be used in the context of trade as 'geographic indicators' can be registered as collective or certification marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rules governing the registration of GIs as certification or collective marks should be determined by Executive Regulations of the Law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of owner of registered mark to prevent confusing use
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner of a registered trademark has the right to prevent others, who do not take approval therefrom, from using a similar or identical trademark, including any geographical indication, in the context of trade, to distinguish products or services that are identical, similar or correlated for which the mark has been registered, in such a way that confuses the consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing emphasizes prevention where use 'in such a way that confuses the consumers' and where goods/services are 'identical, similar or correlated' to the registered mark's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal use and criminal/punitive offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Illegal use of a registered trademark, use of a fake mark, and use of a trademark that falls under certain categories of unregistrable marks are offences punishable under the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several GCC laws criminalize forging or imitating a geographical indication, fraudulent affixation/use, selling goods bearing forged/imitated trade names/GIs, and providing services using forged/imitated trade names/GIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation regulations required for effective GI registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing regulations (by-laws, executive regulations) are required to determine registration rules, the set-up and operation of a Geographical Indications Register, and other procedural details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of implementing regulations in some GCC countries means the registration system is not yet operational (e.g., Bahrain and Qatar pending).

rubrics_metrics.name: Saudi draft law proposed features (TRIPS-aligned definition; registration; scope; term; enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft law aims to provide: a definition of GIs in line with the TRIPS Agreement; a system of GIs registration with legal means for opposition; protection extending to agricultural, industrial, food and handicraft products for local products and for foreign GIs by registering them in the Kingdom if protected in their country of origin; a period of protection for ten years renewable indefinitely; enforcement provisions including precautionary measures, fines and imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional proposed constraints: GIs must conform with Islamic Sharia, public order and morality and not be identical with the common name for such goods or services in Saudi Arabia. Protection would cover GIs of WTO Member countries based on reciprocity; enforcement is ex-officio or at request of any interested party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended EU cooperation actions to build GI systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical actions recommended for EU cooperation: study/virtual visits; conduct surveys on GI awareness; help sectors understand pros/cons; identify GI products with reputation and export potential; share EU best practices and different protection schemes; help authorities develop/adapt laws and regulations; share experience on organizing producers, efficient supply chains, and product specification development; capacity building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original bullet list provided as recommended focus areas for cooperation projects to help GCC countries set up GI systems similar to EU schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Omani GI law
rubrics_metrics.description: Oman: 'The law applies to "any natural or agricultural product or any product of handicraft or industry".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oman has the most comprehensive sui generis law among GCC countries and has been operationally receiving GI registration applications since 2018.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to institute proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Any interested person, or group of producers or consumers, may institute court proceedings to prevent misleading uses or acts of unfair competition concerning GIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standing is articulated in Omani provisions (and similar standing appears across other GCC laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of prohibited uses actionable under GI laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibited acts include: (a) the use of any means in naming or offering any good while hinting the good originated in a different geographical region in a manner that misleads the public; (b) any use that constitutes unfair competition under Article 10bis of the Paris Convention; (c) use of a registered GI not originating in the place indicated, or use in translation or accompanied by 'kind', 'type', 'style', 'imitation' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prohibitions are set out specifically in Omani provisions and mirrored in other GCC laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from GI protection
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are not protected if they: do not comply with the law's definition of GIs; are contrary to public order or morality; are not or cease to be protected in their country of origin; have fallen into disuse; are identical with the term customary in common language as the common name for such goods; are confusingly similar to a mark currently registered or pending registration in good faith; conflict with prior rights acquired under national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions appear across GCC laws (Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait, etc.) and mirror certain TRIPS exceptions; the report notes some TRIPS exceptions (generic names, prior trademark rights, prior use) are missing in some laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: GIs excluded from trademark registrability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some laws explicitly exclude geographical indications from being registrable as trademarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes explicit exclusions (e.g., Sultani Decree No. 67 of 2008 Article 36(c)) and provides that registration as a trademark is prohibited where it would mislead as to origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI registration procedure mirrors trademark procedure (examination and opposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: GI applications in many GCC countries follow the same procedures as trademarks: filing, examination, opposition, cancellation/strike-off, transfer, licensing, seizure and compensation mechanisms; administrative offices (Industrial Property Register) should keep a Geographical Indications Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation often remains pending the issuance of necessary by-laws; examination and an opposition procedure are generally available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against misleading true-but-misleading territorial indications
rubrics_metrics.description: A GI which, although literally true as to the territory, region or locality in which the goods originate, may still be prohibited if it falsely represents to the public that the goods originate in another territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses false impressions even where the literal territorial statement is correct (articulated in GCC laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against GI/trademark conflicts and exploitation of reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A GI that is identical or similar to a trademark for related goods or services can be prohibited if its use is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or to deceive or risk associating the GI with a trademark, or constitutes unfair exploitation of the trademark's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard balances GI rights and trademark rights; the law recognizes likelihood of confusion and reputation exploitation as bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith prior use and name-use exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law allows the use of a GI in good faith by a third party before the GI was granted protection in its country of origin; use of a person's name or predecessor's name is allowed except where it misleads the public; use of a GI not protected or ceased to be protected in its country of origin may be permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are carved-out exceptions to GI enforcement in some GCC laws (Bahrain/Oman examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of protection varies by country (ten years renewable vs unlimited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some laws provide a fixed renewable term (e.g., proposed Saudi draft: ten years renewable indefinitely; Bahrain: ten years renewable for terms of ten years each), while other provisions indicate unlimited protection in certain contexts (report cites an 'unlimited' term in one place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration and renewal rules differ across GCC laws; consistency with TRIPS and practical registrability differ by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homonymous GIs: protection conditioned on consumer non-misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of homonymous geographical indications for goods, protection shall be accorded to each indication provided that consumers are not misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows coexistence of identical names for different places/products where consumer confusion is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial remedies and enforcement powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may grant injunctions to prevent unlawful use of a GI, award damages, and grant appropriate remedies to cover damages resulting from infringements; administrative authorities may also have seizure/precautionary powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringements of registered GIs are punishable offences; remedies include provisional measures and criminal penalties where laws provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: GIs may be protected even without registration (Qatar example)
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are protected in Qatar even if they are not registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates some jurisdictions provide protection based on use/reputation rather than strict registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPS balance and alcohol-related limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS provides higher protection for wines and spirits; GCC countries applying Islamic Sharia that forbids alcoholic beverages are unlikely to recognize or register foreign GIs for wines and spirits on grounds of public order or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes that even if laws comply with TRIPS, additional protection for wines and spirits may be absent due to domestic prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDOs (Protected Designations of Origin) and TSGs (Traditional Specialities Guaranteed)
rubrics_metrics.description: PDOs are product names with the strongest links to place of production; GCC laws do not distinguish between GIs and PDOs (both protected as GIs). TSGs (non-origin labels) protect traditional aspects of products and may be implemented, but collective/certification marks can also serve the role of TSGs in GCC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing PDOs requires cultural readiness, producer associations, technical specifications, and a well-established GI system. Recommendation: EU support to establish basic GI systems before PDO introduction; study potential TSGs as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP enforcement weaknesses: discretion and appeals structure
rubrics_metrics.description: While legal/regulatory systems exist, enforcement is criticized for the degree of discretion given to administrative authorities; some laws introduce quasi-judicial appeals committees appointed by ministers, and most provide for final appeal before civil courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report recommends enhancing effectiveness by addressing discretion and improving judicial review mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional measures under FTAs (seizure; expedited inaudita procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under US FTAs with Bahrain and Oman: parties shall provide civil remedies including provisional measures such as seizure of devices/products suspected of involvement; act on requests for relief inaudita altera parte expeditiously and generally execute within 10 days except in exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These FTA provisions are cited as providing more comprehensive provisional measures in some GCC jurisdictions (Bahrain and Oman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural safeguards for provisional measures (evidence and security)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial authorities may require the plaintiff to provide any reasonably available evidence to satisfy certainty of infringement/imminent infringement, and may order plaintiff to provide reasonable security or equivalent assurance at a level sufficient to protect the defendant and prevent abuse, so as not to unreasonably deter recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These safeguards are part of the FTA-mandated provisional measure regimes and aim to balance rights of plaintiffs and defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttable presumption of patent validity in provisional measures
rubrics_metrics.description: In proceedings concerning provisional measures in relation to enforcement of a patent, each party shall provide for a rebuttable presumption that the patent is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this provision specifically addresses patents under the Oman-US FTA, it is cited in discussing provisional measures and standards of proof applicable in IP enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and trademark laws include provisional/precautionary measures in line with TRIPS
rubrics_metrics.description: GCC copyright and related rights statutes include provisions on provisional and precautionary measures; provisional measures are also provided under the GCC Unified Trademark Law applicable in many GCC countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes alignment with TRIPS standards to a large extent, but practical effectiveness and implementation vary across countries.
